writeBoundary.producer: the TypeScript compiler process (tsc -b --noEmit) and the Vite bundler, run by Vercel's build container on every deployment
writeBoundary.argument: This is the only edge in the repo that both executes an independent analyzer and sits on a path that can block something. The author writes the source; tsc computes the type graph over tsconfig.app.json (include: src) and tsconfig.node.json (include: vite.config.ts, api) with strict:true and emits the exit code. No sentence the author writes changes whether a type error exists. The path to a blocking decision is Vercel zero-config detection: vercel.json sets only function maxDuration and no buildCommand, so Vercel's Vite preset invokes `npm run build`; a non-zero exit from tsc aborts the deployment and the previous alias stays live. Limit: this is the type axis only, and this repo has no test runner of any kind, so nothing anywhere executes the runtime behavior of api/analyze.ts or the React app. Type-correct and wrong is fully reachable here.

evidence: vercel.json contains no buildCommand override -> Vercel Vite preset runs npm run build
repo has no test runner in dependencies or devDependencies

writeBoundary.producer: tsc, but only when a human types the command
writeBoundary.argument: The producer is the same independent compiler as in `build`, so the execution axis is fine — but nothing invokes this script. There is no .github/ directory, no CI config of any kind, and no committed hook (the pre-push hook present in .git/hooks is the auditing machine's local template, not a repo artifact, and it filters branch names, not code). The signal therefore only reaches a decision if the author chooses to run it and chooses to report the result, and I cannot trace that choice. This is the 'test that exists but is not in the pipeline path' case: the identical command is duplicated inside `build`, which is the edge that actually blocks, so classifying this one anchored would double-count a gate it does not own.

It expresses no condition a deployment must satisfy — no buildCommand, no ignoreCommand, no check or protection clause. A deploy gate that ships whatever is pushed asserts nothing about correctness; the timeout budget is a resource limit, not a verdict. The genuine verification content of this deploy lives entirely in the build script it implicitly triggers, judged separately, so counting this node in the denominator would double-count that one edge.

The script's own comment states the correctness rule ('etiqueta SOLO gente que realmente sale en la foto') is enforced by the operator's honesty, and schema.sql confirms the DB will not push back — RLS is enabled with `for all using (true) with check (true)` on every table, so the only DB-side producers are foreign keys and not-null. Writing data you will later display is a claim, not a verification of one.
